changes.old: # Fine-tuning and PEFT Suppose three customers need the same pretrained language model to behave differently: one extracts fields from invoices, another answers support questions, and the third writes summaries. Full fine-tuning can produce three different copies of the weights. With seven billion parameters and two bytes per weight, those copies require 42 GB before serving caches or training state are counted. A shared frozen base plus three small sets of task-specific parameters can reduce that duplication. The model still has to execute the base network for each request. The preceding [[00 Учебник/12 Post-training и Alignment/01 SFT и instruction data|SFT chapter]] defines the training examples, target tokens and loss. A separate choice is which parameters may change when that loss is differentiated. SFT can update all weights, only selected layers, a LoRA branch or a soft prompt. The same parameterization can also be used with a different objective, including DPO. “SFT versus LoRA” therefore compares a training objective with a choice of trainable parameters. ## Choosing the trainable parameters For classification with an encoder, write the prediction as $p(y\mid x)=\operatorname{softmax}(C f_{\theta}(x)+b)$. The pretrained encoder computes a representation $f_\theta(x)$; the new
changes.new: # Fine-tuning and PEFT A 7-billion-parameter model stored at two bytes per weight takes 14 GB. If invoice extraction, support and summarization each get a fully fine-tuned checkpoint, storing the three copies takes 42 GB. With a shared base and three BF16 LoRA adapters of about 4.2 million parameters each, the stored weights instead take 14 GB plus about 25 MB. This counts weight files, not training memory or serving caches. Every request still runs the base network. The [[00 Учебник/12 Post-training и Alignment/01 SFT и instruction data|SFT chapter]] described which tokens contribute to the loss. Here we keep that choice fixed and vary which tensors the optimizer can update. Full fine-tuning updates the original weights. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) updates a smaller set, such as selected layers, added LoRA factors or prefix vectors. Those same parameters can be trained with another loss, such as DPO. The optional CPU listings run in order in one Python session. They check the calculations on small tensors, without pretrained weights. ## Trainable parameters For classification with an encoder, write the prediction as $p(y\mid x)=\operatorname{softmax}(C f_{\theta}(x)+b)$. For multiple customers, merging a different adapter into a separate base copy for each customer loses much of the storage sharing. Keeping adapters unmerged allows a server to share the base and select a branch per request, but those branches have real runtime and scheduling costs. Batched multi-adapter kernels are an implementation problem; algebra does not make task switching free. Likewise, combining factors is not generally the same as combining weight updates: $$ (B_1+B_2)(A_1+A_2) =B_1A_1+B_2A_2+B_1A_2+B_2A_1. $$ The two cross terms are absent from the desired sum of independent updates. changes.new:
assert ns["adapter_parameters"] * 12 / 1e6 == 50.331648
    assert 2400 // 32 * 3 == 225
    assert math.isclose(ns["scale_bits"], .126953125)
    base_parameters = 7_000_000_000
    adapter_parameters = ns["adapter_parameters"]
    full_gb = base_parameters * 12 / 1e9
    bf16_gb = (base_parameters * 2 + adapter_parameters * 12) / 1e9
    quantized_gb = (base_parameters * ((4 + ns["scale_bits"]) / 8)
                    + adapter_parameters * 12) / 1e9
    assert [round(v, 2) for v in (full_gb, bf16_gb, quantized_gb)] == [84, 14.05, 3.66]
    assert round(3 * adapter_parameters * 2 / 1e6) == 25

    # Reusing the toy quantization grid can erase a merged update.
    scalar_base = ns["q_base"][0, 0]
    scalar_delta = torch.tensor(.2, dtype=dtype)
    merged_scalar = scalar_base + scalar_delta
    requantized_scalar = (merged_scalar / ns["q_scale"]).round().clamp(-8, 7) * ns["q_scale"]
    torch.testing.assert_close(merged_scalar, torch.tensor(1.2, dtype=dtype))
    torch.testing.assert_close(requantized_scalar, scalar_base)
    assert not torch.isclose(merged_scalar, requantized_scalar)

    # The published quantized-base example updates only its LoRA factors.
    torch.testing.assert_close(ns["q_codes"], ns["q_codes_before"])
    torch.testing.assert_close(ns["q_base"], torch.diag(torch.tensor([1., 2.], dtype=dtype)))
